title: King's Indian Defense
description: The famous system opening for Black which can be played against every single White opening besides e4.

r1b1r1k1/1p1n1pbp/1qpp1np1/p5B1/2P1P3/1N.text:
But we can ignore that threat and go for ...a5!

White shouldn't capture on d6 because ...a4 is strong, dislodging the knight and leaving the b2-pawn weak again.

All in all, we've got a comfortable position here and plenty to hope for.

r1b1r1k1/pp1n1pbp/1qpp1np1/6B1/2P1P3/1NN.text:
White defends it with Nb3. 

The queen is also eyeing our d6-pawn now.

r1bq1rk1/pppn1pb1/3p1npp/8/2PQP2B/2N2N2/.text:
The bishop naturally retreats to h4.

Usually pushing pawns in front of your king is dangerous, but the KID is famous for being an extremely solid opening.

So we can afford to continue pushing and chasing the bishop away!

r1bq1rk1/pppn1pbp/3p1np1/6B1/2PQP3/2N2N2.text:
White now pins our knight on f6.

It's already sufficiently defended, but we should remove the pin. 

So we will attack it with ...h6.

r1bqr1k1/1p1n1pbp/p1pp1np1/8/2PNP3/2N1BP.text:
We'll slowly prepare ...d5 on the next move.

We could lose a pawn there, but then we've got ...Nb6 to get it back immediately.

r1bqr1k1/pp1n1pbp/2pp1np1/6B1/2PNP3/2N2P.text:
The bishop arrives on g5 and pins our knight.

We will unpin immediately and improve the queen, attacking the b2-pawn.

r1bqr1k1/pp1n1pbp/2pp1np1/8/2PNP3/2N1BP2.text: White goes for Be3 now, occupying the diagonal.

r1bqr1k1/pp1n1pbp/6p1/3p4/3NP3/3BBP2/PP4.text:
Our position is very comfortable.

A nice idea from here would be to transfer the knight to f6, but it can also go to e5 or c5.

r1bqr1k1/pppn1pb1/3p1n1p/6p1/2PQP3/2N2NB.text:
We've expanded on the kingside with tempo and have some grasp over the center.

It's time to improve the rook and strengthen our central control.

Our plans will consist of going after the e4-pawn with ...Nc5 as well.

Our f-knight could jump to h5 to attack the bishop on g3.

r1bqr1k1/pppn1pbp/3p1np1/8/2PNP3/2N2B2/P.text:
But after ...Nbd7 we get a lot of activity and ideas such as ...Ne5 or ...Nc5.

If White tries something like Bg5 here, we can chase away the bishop with ...h6 and ...g5. Even ...g4!? works after that.

rn1qr1k1/pp1b1pbp/6p1/1B1p4/3NP3/4BP2/PP.text:
Which we will do.

White will most likely trade here, after which both recaptures are fine.

Recapturing with the knight leads to putting the knight on f6, or even b6 and c4.

Recapturing with the queen leads to some nice attacks against White's center.

rnb1r1k1/1pq2pbp/p1pp1np1/8/N1PNP3/2B2P2.text:
But now White's knight is quite uncomfortable on a4 as we prepare ...b5.

Over the next few moves, we'll develop our queenside pieces and look for central pawn strikes.

Also, ...Nh5 to ...Nf4 is in the air.

rnb1r1k1/pp3pbp/1qpp1np1/6B1/N1PNP3/5P2/.text:
White tries to fight against our threats with tempo.

But we will just sidestep to a5 and attack the bishop on g5.

rnb1r1k1/pp3pbp/2p3p1/6q1/2BNPn2/2N2P2/P.text:
Now our queen is threatening checkmate on g5, which will prove to be devastating in the long run.

White should have captured our knight on move 12!

rnb1r1k1/pp3pbp/2pp1np1/q7/N1PNP3/5P2/PP.text:
Once White retreats to d2, we will have to move our queen again, but we've managed to push White's pieces back and relieve a lot of pressure.

Now our queen is safe and we are still threatening ...Nxe4!

rnb1r1k1/ppq2pbp/2pp1np1/8/N1PNP3/2B2P2/.text: That's why White defends the knight with Bc3.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/2PPP3/2N2N2/P.text:
One of the most natural moves now is Be2, simply activating the bishop and getting ready to castle.

In the King's Indian Defense, you should always look for pawn breaks such as ...e5 or ...c5 after having developed the kingside.

We have to contest the center at some point in order to help our pieces develop and prosper, so we will strike with ...e5 now!

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/4p3/2PPP3/2N2N2/.text:
Study 1 deals with White castling, which happens 44% of the time.

This not only hides the king, but is a waiting move of sorts, since White is giving us the choice to capture on d4.

And that's what we will do.

Splitting White's central pawns and leaving the e5-square for our pieces if needed is the way to go.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/8/2PNP3/2N5/PP2B.text:
White recaptures with the knight, centralizing it.

Their e4-pawn is now weaker, and there are no prospects of pushing e5, so we should make it our primary target with ...Re8.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/8/2PQP3/2N2N2/PP.text:
White decides to capture on d4 with the queen.

They want to leave their queen in the center if possible.

Now we are going for a move that is played just 18% of the time (against ...Nc6 which is played 70% of the time) and scores very well for Black, which is ...Nbd7.

It controls the center but also supports our f6-knight and leaves room for the c-pawn to potentially move.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/2PPP3/2N2N2/PP.text:
Developing both knights after expanding in the center is the most standard way to continue, and you should face it 30% of the time.

White wants to finish kingside development next.

In response, we are already able to castle, so that's exactly what we will do.

rnbqk2r/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2PPP3/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
Three pawns in the center is what you will encounter the most often, since it's chosen 55% of the time in this position.

It's usually a good idea to grab as much central space as you can in the opening.

However, we will start to combat this soon.

For now, we will play ...d6 and take control of the e5-square, since we don't want to allow White more space than we already have.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White plays the most popular move in this position, which is 3.Nc3.

It's played 77% of the time, and was seen in more than 28 million games.

The knight now controls the e4-square and White is preparing e4.

We'll respond naturally with the fianchetto of the dark-squared bishop and prepare to castle.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Since White couldn't play e4 because of our knight, they expand in the next best possible way: c4!

The two pawns occupy a lot of central space and are trying to suffocate our development.

The King's Indian Defense is famous for Black giving up the center early and then trying to win it back with a pawn break in the center.

So, we will play ...g6 since we want to fianchetto our bishop on g7.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to the first study of our King's Indian Defense course!

In Chapter 1, we will delve deep into the main lines of the KID with White pushing all three pawns in the center, developing the kingside quickly, and, in this study, castling on move 7.

The first move of our King's Indian Defense is the flexible 1...Nf6.

We develop our knight to the f6-square, controlling e4.

rnbqr1k1/1p3pbp/p5p1/3p4/4P3/2N1BP2/PP2B.text:
White had to go back to d4.

Jumping to c3 loses.

rnbqr1k1/1p3pbp/p5p1/8/3pP3/2N1BP2/PP2B1.text:
Now we can play ...d4 with a fork!

We are going to win a piece and soon the game.

rnbqr1k1/pp3pbp/2p2np1/3P4/3NP3/2N1BP2/P.text:
White captures on d5 with the c-pawn.

Recapturing with the pawn is fine, but I like taking with the knight here.

It's tricky since White's pieces are vulnerable on the e-file.

rnbqr1k1/pp3pbp/2p3p1/3N4/3NP3/4BP2/PP2B.text:
White trades the knights.

It wasn't really smart for them to take with the e-pawn.

We will simply recapture, of course.

rnbqr1k1/pp3pbp/2p3p1/3n4/3NP3/2N2P2/PP2.text:
Declining this sacrifice by moving the bishop away simply leads to an inferior position for White.

Instead of trading the knights, we can improve to f4 and put some pressure on the light-squared bishop.

rnbqr1k1/pp3pbp/2p3p1/8/2BNPn2/2N2P2/PP3.text: Placing the bishop on c4 might seem logical, but it's a losing blunder.

rnbqr1k1/pp3pbp/2pp1np1/6B1/2PNP3/2N2P2/.text:
You can expect to see Bg5 at some point.

Remember what I said about the diagonal opening up after ...c6?

Well, now we will place the queen on b6 and pin the White knight to the king!

We are threatening both to capture on b2 as well as a nasty tactic with ...Nxe4, which would leave the d4-knight weak!

rnbqr1k1/pp3pbp/2pp1np1/8/2PNP3/2N1BP2/P.text:
The mistake White often makes is Be3.

The bishop occupies the diagonal and defends against ...Qb6, but White forgets our other, main idea.

We push in the center!

The position will open up soon, and hopefully in our favor.

rnbqr1k1/pp3pbp/2pp1np1/8/2PNP3/2N2P2/PP.text:
White could play Kh1 in this position, which is actually the best move.

The king is off the diagonal and prevents any tricks from us.

We'll just develop the knight to the standard d7-square in response and await White's next move.

rnbqr1k1/pp3pbp/6p1/1B1p4/3NP3/4BP2/PP4P.text:
The most common move at this point is Bb5.

White attacks our rook and is trying to make us block the attack.

rnbqr1k1/pp3pbp/6p1/1N1p4/4P3/4BP2/PP2B1.text:
Trying to move the knight away so that the queen could potentially capture on d5 doesn't work.

First, we will just attack the knight.

rnbqr1k1/pp3pbp/6p1/3p4/3NP3/3BBP2/PP4PP.text: Defending the position like this is pretty solid, although we get a slight advantage.

rnbqr1k1/ppp2pb1/3p1n1p/6p1/2PNP3/2N3B1/.text: Once the bishop lands on g3, White's plans have failed and their e4-pawn is hanging.

rnbqr1k1/ppp2pb1/3p1npp/8/2PNP2B/2N5/PP2.text: After the bishop retreats to h4, we can continue chasing it with ...g5!

rnbqr1k1/ppp2pb1/3p3p/6p1/2PNn3/2N3B1/PP.text: We will capture it with the knight and we are simply up a pawn with a better position.

rnbqr1k1/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/6B1/2PNP3/2N5/PP.text:
White tries pinning our knight, but this is an inaccuracy.

We can simply chase away the bishop right now.

We will attack it with ...h6 first.

rnbqr1k1/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/8/2PNP3/2N2P2/PP.text:
Protecting the e4-pawn with f3 is by far the most popular move (played 75% of the time).

It does strengthen the center, but it has some drawbacks on its own.

Let's play ...c6 for now and potentially prepare ...d5.

This also opens up the b6-square for our queen to occupy the diagonal which has just opened up.

Black wins 53% of the games in this position, and what's funny is that White makes a mistake over 40% of the time with their next move!

r1b2rk1/1pp2pb1/3p1qpp/p1nPp3/2P1P3/P1N2.text:
But now our queen lands on f6.

If White plays b4, you can trade a few of the queenside pieces, and then move the queen to prepare ...f5.

The ...f5-break is actually pretty common in the KID as the opener for a kingside attack!

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pb1/3p1Bpp/p1nPp3/2P1P3/P1N.text: White is basically forced to capture in this line.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pb1/n2p1npp/p2Pp3/2P1P2B/2N.text:
And it's time to bring out our queenside knight.

We have plenty of ideas, involving ...Nc5 as mentioned, as well as ...Bd7 and ...Qe8 to unpin and connect on the light squares.

Our f6-knight can then either improve forward or jump backwards to h7, trying to find a better spot.

Sometimes, even ...g5!? is an idea.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pbp/3p1np1/2nPp3/p1P1P3/P1N.text:
We have ...a4 now, since the a-pawn is defended twice!

White won't be pushing b4 any time soon.

Our knight on c5 even has opportunities of transfering to the d4-square via b3 now.

The bishop will be activated on d7, and we can also keep in mind some kingside ideas with ...f5.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pbp/3p1np1/p1nPp1B1/2P1P3/P.text:
Pinning our knight instead of defending the pawn directly is certainly an option.

As per usual, we will attack the bishop immediately.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pbp/3p1np1/p1nPp3/2P1P3/P1N.text:
The queen improves to c2 and defends the pawn.

Logical, but...

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pbp/n2p1np1/p2Pp3/2P1P3/2N1.text:
It's logical for White to try and stop ...Nc5 by placing the bishop on e3.

That's why it makes sense for us to attack that bishop!

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pbp/n2p1np1/p2Pp3/2P1P3/P1N.text:
Going for a3 prepares b4 but seems to be one move too slow.

Our knight jumps to c5 anyway and attacks the vulnerable e4-pawn.

White has to defend it and doesn't have time for b4 now.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pbp/n2p2p1/p2Pp1B1/2P1P1n1/.text:
You can expect White to attack your queen once your knight moves away from f6.

There's nothing to worry about as ...f6 is fine since it comes with tempo.

Even though we block our dark-squared bishop, we don't need it for now.

r1bq1rk1/1pp3b1/n2p1pp1/p2Pp2p/2P1P1nB/2.text:
It's important to play ...h5 before you retreat with ...Nh6 and ...Nf7.

It helps our kingside attack which could come later, and restricts White.

Apart from that, our queenside knight will be coming to c5.

r1bq1rk1/1pp3bp/n2p1pp1/p2Pp3/2P1P1nB/2N.text: White retreats, and here's a move to remember.

rnbq1rk1/1pp2pb1/3p1npp/p2Pp3/2P1P2B/2N2.text: The bishop retreats to h4 now.

rnbq1rk1/1pp2pbp/3p1np1/p2Pp1B1/2P1P3/2N.text:
Going for 8.Bg5 is pretty harmless, but it's important to play ...h6 quickly when it happens.

We don't want to give White any more time.

rnbq1rk1/1pp2pbp/3p1np1/p2Pp3/2P1P3/2N2N.text:
White decides to castle, which is solid but gives us space and time to proceed with our plans.

And we will start with the knight on a6, eyeing that c5-square.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/2PPP3/2N2N2/P.text:
One of the most natural moves is Be2.

We will strike with ...e5 now to fight in the center.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/3Pp3/2P1P3/2N2N2.text:
This study analyzes positions after 7.d5, which arise 30% of the time.

This move is ambitious as it gives up the c5-square and closes down the center, but tries to suffocate us by controlling c6 and e6.

To come up with a suitable plan against this, we will play ...a5 in order to prevent  the quick b4 and c5.

Our ideas usually involve ...Nbd7 or ...Na6, aiming for the c5-square.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/2PPP3/2N2N2/PP.text:
White wants to finish kingside development next.

We are already able to castle, so that's exactly what we will do.

rnbqk2r/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2PPP3/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
Three pawns in the center is what you will encounter most often.

We will play ...d6 and take control of the e5-square.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
Developing the queenside knight first.

We'll respond naturally with the fianchetto of the dark-squared bishop and prepare to castle.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Two pawns in the center by White.

White opens with d4.

We recapture with the bishop.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2pbp/2n2np1/4p1B1/2P1P3/2N2N.text:
We have the same remedy as in other variations - we simply slide the rook to the e-file. 

Our plans in this position can include kicking the bishop out with ...h6–g5, and placing our knight on the d4 square. Our light-squared bishop will go to g4.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2pbp/5np1/2n1N1B1/2P1P3/2N2P.text:
White defends e4 with their f-pawn.

But we can take it anyway with our f-knight. It’s a discovered attack on their knight!

r1b1r1k1/ppp2pbp/6p1/2n1N1B1/2P1N3/5P2/P.text:
White recaptures with their knight.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2pbp/6p1/4N1B1/2P1P3/8/PP2B1.text: White recaptures with the f-pawn, reaching a position with an isolated pawn.

White captures our e5-pawn with their knight.

This isn't a free piece: White has Rd8+ and Bxf6 tactics to recover the piece if we capture the knight.

We improve our knight, placing it on a more active square and threatening to capture on e4.

r1bQ1rk1/ppp2pbp/2n2np1/4p3/2P1P3/2N2N2/.text:
White can trade the queens.

We recapture with the rook.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1pbp/2p2np1/4p1B1/2P1P3/2N2.text:
We remove the option for White to place any piece on the d5 square.

r1br2k1/ppp2pbp/2n2np1/4p1B1/2P1P3/2N2N2.text: Black develops the bishop, and pins our knight to the rook.

rnb1r1k1/pp3pbp/2p3p1/3Pp1B1/2B1P3/5N2/P.text:
White improves their light-squared bishop, aiming to recapture the pawn with the bishop.

We take their central pawn.

rnb1r1k1/ppp2p1p/6p1/4b1B1/2P1N3/8/PP2BP.text:
We have the same remedy as in other variations where White puts pressure on our rook - we slide it to the e-file. 

If White plays Bf6, we have to be careful not to blunder a fork on f6.

Our plan could be ...Nc6, ...Be6 or ...Bf5, and bringing the rooks to the e- and d-files.

rnb1r1k1/ppp2pbp/5np1/3Np1B1/2P1P3/5N2/P.text:
White jumps forward with the knight to the d5 square, improving the piece, adding pressure on f6, and threatening the fork on c7. This is the most played move in the position - 41% of the time.

The only way to defend against the threats is to capture the knight.

rnb1r1k1/ppp2pbp/5np1/4p1B1/2P1P3/2N2N2/.text:
27% of players go for opposite-side castling, leading to an interesting and dynamic game.

Now ...Na6. Our idea is to get the knight to the c5-square. Our plans also include ...c6, preventing any piece from reaching the d5-square, and kicking the bishop back with ...h6.

rnb1r1k1/ppp2pbp/6p1/3Pp1B1/4P3/5N2/PP2B.text:
White recaptures with the c-pawn.

And we immediately undermine it with our c-pawn. The only challenge is Bc4 - if dxc6, we play Nxc6, recapturing while developing.

rnbQ1rk1/ppp2pbp/5np1/4p3/2P1P3/2N2N2/PP.text:
At the amateur level, most players go for the queen trade in this position, it appears in 72% of games.

We recapture with the rook.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/2PPP3/2N2N2/P.text:
As in the previous chapter, White develops their light-squared bishop to e2.

We are ready to strike in the center with ...e5. It may look like we're simply losing a pawn, but we'll see that we aren’t.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/4P3/2P1P3/2N2N2/.text:
White immediately captures on e5 with their pawn - this is the subject of study in this chapter.

About 15% of games go like this.

We recapture.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/5np1/4p3/2P1P3/2N2N2/PP.text:
White can also delay the queen trade and simply castle. This occurs 12% of the time.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/2PPP3/2N2N2/PP.text:
White develops their other knight.

rnbqk2r/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2PPP3/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
White occupies more central space with e4, and builds a broad pawn center.

We play ...d6 to discourage White from pushing their central pawns further and to prepare a central strike with ...e5 or ...c5.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
White brings out the queen’s knight, developing naturally and controlling the center.

We continue with our plan, fianchettoing our bishop. We don’t mind if White occupies the entire center.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White pushes the c-pawn, gaining more space and central control.

2...g6. We aim to fianchetto our bishop and place it on the long diagonal.

rnbr2k1/ppp2Nbp/6p1/8/2P1n3/2N5/PP2BPPP/.text:
White might think they’re winning by capturing on f7 - but it actually blunders a piece!

It only works if we take the knight on f7 first, which is not our plan.

Still, it’s surprisingly common - played in 37% of games.

Our winning move is to take their c3 knight with check!

rnbr2k1/ppp2p1p/6p1/4b1B1/2P1N3/8/PP2BPP.text: White develops their bishop, leaving the b2-pawn undefended but attacking our rook. Danger levels.

rnbr2k1/ppp2pbp/5np1/4N3/2P1P3/2N5/PP2BP.text:
White may also capture on e5, which looks like a free pawn - but we’ll recover it immediately, reaching an equal position.

This capture is played in 18% of games.

59% of players will take our knight.

Another option is to give up the bishop for the knight - played in 17% of cases.

The bishop keeps retreating.

Pushing the e-pawn in the center is rare, seen in just 4% of games.

White prevents any piece from landing on the g4-square - the best move according to the engine - but it’s only seen in 9% of games.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/2PPP3/2NB1N2/.text:

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/5np1/4P3/2P5/2N2N2/PP3.text:
White recaptures with the e-pawn, attacking our knight.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2p1p/6p1/4b3/2P1N3/3B4/PP3PP.text:
And we recover the piece.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/3Pp3/2P1P3/2N2N1.text:

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/3Pp3/2P1P3/2NB1N.text: White chooses to close the center by pushing the d-pawn forward in 59% of games.

White trades pawns in the center 18% of the time.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/5np1/4N3/2P1P3/2NB4/PP3.text:
White will take our pawn on e5, but we have the same trick as in the last chapter - a discovered attack on the knight.

We capture White’s e4-pawn.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/2PPP3/2N2N2/PP.text:
White brings out their other knight.

rnbqk2r/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2PPP3/2N5/PP3PPP.text:

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:

rnbq1rk1/5pbp/P4np1/3P4/4p3/2N2N2/PP2B1P.text: Black has temporarily sacrificed two pawns (a6 is easily recovered) but has a nice position. Black will play Qb6 and try to keep White's king in the center. Black's e-pawn is difficult for White to take, because this would open the e-file.

If they go for d5, we'll undermine it further with ...e6.

Otherwise, we can trade on d4 and develop with ...Nc6.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/2PP4/5NP1/PP2.text:
White castles.

We go ...Nc6 because the knight may be repositioned to a5.

rnbq1rk1/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2PP4/5NP1/PP2PP.text:
White prepares to castle.

Now it's time to push ...d6 and prepare for a break with ...c5.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/2PPP3/2N2P2/PP.text:
White has been only pushing pawns, so they start to bring out their pieces.

We castle, and we have achieved our setup.

rnbqk2r/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2PP4/5NP1/PP2PP1.text:
White goes for a Catalan setup with a kingside fianchetto as well.

We'll get the king into safety.

rnbqk2r/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2PPP3/5P2/PP4PP/.text:
White grabs the center.

...d6 also prevents White from pushing e5 in some cases.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/5np1/2pP4/2P4P/8/PP2PP.text: White wants to keep the center closed.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp2/5np1/2pP3p/2P4P/8/PP2PP.text: We stop White's kingside attacking ideas and now can proceed with ideas similar to the Samisch: Bg7, d6, 0-0 and the critical pawn breaks e6 and b5.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP3P/8/PP2PPP1.text:
This is a very rare move, played a few times by GMs. 

White tries to initiate a quick attack on our kingside. 

When our opponent starts an attack on the kingside, it is a good idea to take some action in the center. Here, we'll play ...c5.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP4/5N2/PP2PPP.text:
This is the second most popular choice for White, with little over 4 million games played.

Let's fianchetto here.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2PP4/5P2/PP2P1P.text:
This is a high level move seen at the master level. 

White's idea is to avoid the Grunfeld defense, which we had no intentions of playing anyway, so let's just play the way we do against the Samisch.

Let's get the bishop fianchettoed.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White grabs some central squares.

We will fianchetto.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
This study deals with all the lines from move 3 that do not involve Nc3.

White goes for 1.d4.

...Nf6 to initiate the King's Indian.

1rbq1rk1/1p2ppbp/p1np1np1/2p5/P1P1P3/2NP.text: White tries to shut down our plan of pushing the b-pawn.

1rbqnrk1/1p2ppbp/p1np2p1/2p5/P1P1P3/2NP2.text: This move opens up the bishop's line of sight and potentially prepares ...Nd4!?. We may also play ...Nc7 to support the ...b7-b5 push.

r1bq1rk1/1p2ppbp/p1np1np1/2p5/2P1P3/2NP2.text:
White also makes a waiting move that restricts the g4 square.

We move our rook to b8. It will prepare b7-b5.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2n2np1/2pp4/4P3/3P1NP1/.text:
White adds another supporter to the e-pawn and threatens to push it forward.

We block the pawn and take the full center.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2np1np1/2p5/2P1P3/2NP2P.text:
Black has very strong control over the d4 square, so White usually settles for playing d3 here (60% of the time).

...a6 is a flexible move, restricting White's knight and preparing to support b7-b5.

r1bq1rk1/pp3pbp/2n2np1/2pPp3/8/3P1NP1/PP.text:
White trades a pair of central pawns.

We recapture. Once the knight moves, e5 gets another defender in the form of the g7-bishop.

r1bq1rk1/pp3pbp/2n3p1/2pnp3/2N5/3P1NP1/P.text:
10.Nc4 is played over 50% of the time here. White has three attackers on e5, and we have two defenders.

...f6 is an interesting approach, reinforcing the center with a pawn, and simultaneously stopping White from putting a piece on g5.

r1bq1rk1/pp4bp/2n2pp1/2pnp3/P1N5/3P1NP1/.text:
White expands on the queenside.

The light-squared bishop will be good on e6, where it covers some of the light squares that we weakened by playing ...f7-f6.

r2q1rk1/3n1pb1/2ppbnpp/4p3/2P5/2NP1NP1/4.text: Black recaptures, with a rock-solid position. After connecting rooks and finishing development, we will prepare to break in the center with d6-d5.

r2q1rk1/pp4bp/2n1bpp1/2pnp3/P1N5/2PP1NP1.text: c3 prepares to eventually break with d3-d4.

r4rk1/pp1q2bp/2n1bpp1/2pnp3/P1N5/2PP1NP1.text:
Reinforcing the loose bishop and unpinning the e5 pawn.

Black has a very solid position. In some lines we will play ...Rf7 and reroute the bishop to f8, where it will be less caged in. Other common ideas involve playing ...Rad8 and ...b6.

rn1q1rk1/1p3pb1/2ppbnpp/1P2p3/2P5/2NP1NP.text:
White often continues pushing their queenside pawns.

We finish developing our pieces.

rnb2rk1/pp3pb1/2pp1qpp/4p3/2P5/2NP1NP1/P.text: Black has a solid position and the bishop pair. The queen will typically retreat to e7 or d8, and after developing the remaining pieces to natural squares, Black can consider expanding with moves like ...f5 or ... a5.

rnbq1rk1/1p3pb1/2pp1npp/4p3/1PP5/2NP1NP1.text:
White takes back.

We develop the light-squared bishop to e6, where it may potentially support d6-d5 in the distant future.

rnbq1rk1/1p3pb1/2pp1npp/p3p3/1PP5/P1NP1N.text:
White plays the move they have been preparing.

We take the pawn.

rnbq1rk1/1p3pbp/2pp1np1/p3p3/2P5/P1NP1NP.text:
White prepares b2-b4.

...h6 is a flexible waiting move, giving the king another square and restricting White's dark-squared bishop and knight.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/3p1np1/2p5/2P1P3/2N3P1/.text:
White castles.

Now that the c-pawn has advanced, we can put the knight on c6 without worrying about blocking the pawn.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/2pp4/4P3/3P1NP1/PP.text:
White strikes at our central pawns, just as we would when playing e7-e5 in a main line King's Indian Defense.

We continue developing our queenside knight to c6. Note that e4-e5 can be met with Ng4, which would attack the pawn three times.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pb1/2pp1Bpp/4p3/2P5/2NP1NP1/.text: The most common move (44%) is to capture. White cannot play Bh4 and maintain the pin, as we can trap the bishop with g6-g5.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/2pp1np1/4p1B1/2P5/2NP1NP.text:
Played about 26% of the time. White develops a piece and pins the Black knight.

With 8...h6, we immediately ask White's bishop to commit.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/2pp1np1/4p3/2P5/2NP1NP1/.text:
Rb1 is also played about 26% of the time.

We will play ...a5. White's idea is to expand on the queenside, and so we prepare to meet b2-b4 by capturing the pawn.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/2P1P3/2N3P1/P.text:
If White plays Nf3, the position will likely transpose into something we have seen before.

We recommend the move ...c5 here.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/2P5/2N2NP1/PP.text:
White castles.

White has decided to delay playing e2-e4 or d2-d4, so now we can start occupying the center ourselves.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3p4/8/3P1NP1/PPPN.text:
White develops a piece to a natural square.

We continue taking central space.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/4p3/2P5/2NP1NP1/.text:
7.d3 is played here 48% of the time.

Note that 7.d4, played 30% of the time, transposes back into a previously studied line after ...Nc6 (see Chapter 5).

Black has many choices, but ...c6 is a nice move, blunting White's light-squared bishop and restricting the c3 knight.

rnbq1rk1/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2P1P3/2N3P1/PP1.text:
White plays 5. e4 here about 27% of the time.

As is typical in the King's Indian Defense, we play ...d6 to restrict the e-pawn, open up the d7 square, and control e5 and c5.

rnbq1rk1/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2P5/2N2NP1/PP1P.text:
5.Nf3 is played about 27% of the time here.

...d6 is still a good move here, controlling some central squares, opening up the d7 square for our knight or bishop, and potentially looking to play e7-e5 or c7-c5.

rnbq1rk1/ppppppbp/5np1/8/8/3P1NP1/PPP1PP.text:
By playing d3, White has played exactly the setup that we usually play.

One approach here is to play ...d5 instead of ...d6, occupying the center, since White has forgotten about the center. In doing so, we break the symmetry of the position.

rnbqk2r/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2P5/2N3P1/PP1PPP.text:
White fianchettoes their bishop.

We get our king to safety. We do not need ...d6 yet.

rnbqk2r/ppppppbp/5np1/8/8/5NP1/PPPPPPBP/.text:
White castles. 

This is standard procedure in the Reti. 

It gives us time to castle as well and achieve our setup.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2P5/2N3P1/PP1PP.text:
In many of White's setups in the English Opening, the light-squared bishop is fianchettoed.

We fianchetto our bishop, continuing to our King's Indian setup.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/8/5NP1/PPPPPPBP.text: White fianchettoes their bishop, and we will do the same.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPPP.text:
White develops a knight towards the center.

We prepare our fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/8/5NP1/PPPPPP1P/.text:
One possible way White can play is with the King's Indian Attack: that is, playing the King's Indian setup themselves. In this variation, we will explore what we can do in response to this.

We start by fianchettoing our bishop as usual.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/RNB.text:
The King's Indian setup is quite flexible, and can be played against the English Opening (1. c4) as well. In many lines, it transposes into a variation we have already studied. 

Here, we look at how to play against a typical English opening setup. We start with ...Nf6.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/5N2/PPPPPPPP/RNB.text:
1.Nf3 is a flexible move from White, delaying the commitment of any central pawns and asking to see what setup Black is going for first.

We can still play the King's Indian Defense against 1.Nf3. There are many setups that White can employ, including transposing into lines we've covered in previous chapters. We will develop the knight as well.
